recent_posts.title: How Mythos Signals Cybersecurity Disruption
recent_posts.summary: Anthropic's unreleased AI model Mythos is raising serious cybersecurity alarms due to its ability to discover vulnerabilities at unprecedented scale, automatically create exploits, and chain lesser vulnerabilities together. Before release, it found thousands of new vulnerabilities across major OSes and browsers — including one that had existed undetected for 27 years. Mozilla's Firefox testing showed Mythos found 271 bugs where the previous Claude model found 22. Extrapolating from 2025's ~50,000 CVEs, widespread Mythos access could yield over 600,000 vulnerabilities annually. The core threat is the collapse of Time-to-Exploit windows: current monthly patch cycles like Microsoft's Patch Tuesday become obsolete when AI can find, exploit, and attack within hours. The author argues defenders must urgently adopt AI-driven security tools and shift toward continuous patching models, while acknowledging the industry has no clear roadmap for adapting to this new reality.

recent_posts.title: Why AI-speed threats demand a containment-first security posture
recent_posts.summary: AI-powered offensive tools like Anthropic's Claude Mythos are collapsing the time between vulnerability discovery and exploitation from weeks to hours, fundamentally breaking prevention-first security models. The post argues organizations must shift to a containment-first, breach-ready posture centered on microsegmentation to limit lateral movement and blast radius. It outlines five practical pillars: assume compromise, make lateral movement expensive via Zero Trust and microsegmentation, gain full IT/OT/IoT visibility, continuously reduce attack surface, and build machine-speed response playbooks. ColorTokens Xshield is presented as the platform enabling this posture.

recent_posts.title: Why AI agent security governance is missing half the attack surface
recent_posts.summary: Noma Security's 'Lethal by Design' report exposes a critical asymmetry in AI agent security: while MCP servers produce auditable logs, the 'Skills' that drive agent reasoning leave no forensic trail. Analysis of enterprise deployments found 76% of MCP servers carry high-risk capabilities, and 60% of both MCPs and Skills can cause irreversible state changes. Real-world incidents — including an Amazon Q filesystem wipe via GitHub PR injection and Replit's AI agent destroying a production database — demonstrate that Meta's 'Rule of Two' framework fails to prevent autonomous destruction. Noma proposes the No Excessive CAP framework, focusing on three controllable levers: Capabilities (whitelist only required tools), Autonomy (gate high-blast-radius actions behind human approval), and Permissions (minimum-privilege, expiring credentials). These three dimensions interact multiplicatively, making their combined misconfiguration the highest-risk configuration in enterprise AI deployments.

recent_posts.title: ShinyHunters Claims Responsibility for Breach of EdTech Company Instructure
recent_posts.summary: The ShinyHunters extortion group has claimed responsibility for a breach of Instructure, the company behind the Canvas learning management platform. The group claims to have stolen 3.65 TB of data affecting up to 275 million students, teachers, and staff across nearly 15,000 institutions globally, including private messages, names, email addresses, and student IDs. Instructure confirmed the breach, revoked credentials, rotated keys, and restored most services by May 3. This is the second ShinyHunters attack on Instructure in under a year — a previous breach occurred in September 2025. The incident underscores a broader trend of ransomware groups shifting from encryption-based extortion to data-theft extortion, making education institutions increasingly attractive targets due to regulatory and reputational exposure.

recent_posts.title: Handling User Documents Securely in Authentication and Onboarding Systems
recent_posts.summary: Secure document handling during user onboarding requires more than a clean login flow. When products need identity proof — such as address documents, signed forms, or business registrations — files must be governed from upload to deletion. Key practices include defining file type/size rules, limiting reviewer access to only necessary fields, masking sensitive data, logging all actions, and setting retention/deletion policies. Connecting document review with account signals (verified email, device history, profile details) helps reviewers prioritize attention without rejecting ordinary mismatches. Tools like PDF-to-Word converters can assist review workflows but must operate within controlled, auditable processes rather than ad-hoc email or shared drives.

recent_posts.title: AI for Security Infrastructure: Rebalancing Cybersecurity for the Decade Ahead
recent_posts.summary: Modern cybersecurity has been dominated by reactive 'assume breach' thinking, leaving security architects under-resourced while configuration drift, tool sprawl, and dynamic threat exposure create growing risk. General-purpose LLMs are unreliable for security tasks due to hallucinations and lack of domain-specific reasoning. Domain-Specific Language Models (DSLMs), trained exclusively on validated security data and frameworks like MITRE and NIST, offer deterministic, hallucination-free reasoning for security architecture tasks. DSLMs enable proactive misconfiguration detection and remediation, shifting cybersecurity strategy from reactive incident response toward prevention-first approaches that reduce breach frequency and free up security teams.

recent_posts.title: Is reposting the '86 47' meme a criminal threat under First Amendment law
recent_posts.summary: Analysis of the reported DOJ indictment of James Comey for reposting a '86 47' seashell meme, examined through the lens of Supreme Court 'true threats' jurisprudence. Drawing on Elonis v. United States (2015) and Counterman v. Colorado (2023), the piece argues the prosecution is constitutionally precarious because both rulings require proof of at least recklessness — that the speaker consciously disregarded a substantial risk their communication would be perceived as threatening. The Comey meme is indirect, symbolic, untargeted, and linguistically ambiguous, making it weaker than the Counterman case, which still failed to sustain a conviction. The analysis warns that extending criminal liability to such ambiguous political expression would dangerously expand the 'true threats' category and blur the line between protected speech and criminal conduct.

recent_posts.title: How AutoSecT Uses AI to Find Vulnerabilities That Actually Matter
recent_posts.summary: AutoSecT is an AI-driven penetration testing and vulnerability management platform built by Kratikal that addresses alert fatigue by going beyond static CVSS scores. It validates whether detected vulnerabilities are actually exploitable in a given environment, applies context-aware risk prioritization based on asset criticality and real-world threat intelligence, and delivers tailored patch recommendations. The platform covers web apps, mobile apps, cloud infrastructure (AWS, GCP, Azure), APIs, and network security from a single interface, integrating with JIRA, Slack, and Microsoft Teams to move vulnerabilities through remediation workflows rather than static reports.

recent_posts.title: AI slop is not a new problem it is just a new scapegoat
recent_posts.summary: A short opinion piece arguing that the backlash against AI-generated 'slop' is really about resentment over skipping the creative struggle, not actual quality concerns. The author points out that low-quality, thoughtless writing has always existed from human authors — vendor whitepapers, LinkedIn posts, security marketing — and that AI is just a new target for an old frustration. Writing automation has existed for decades (spell checkers, grammar tools, templates), and the real issue is a perceived lack of earned suffering rather than a genuine quality problem.

recent_posts.title: 4 ransomware warning signs K-12 IT teams should monitor
recent_posts.summary: K-12 schools are increasingly targeted by ransomware attacks due to large user populations and limited IT resources. Four key early warning signs IT teams should monitor are: unusual login activity (unfamiliar IPs, failed attempts, off-hours access), unexpected file encryption (mass file modifications or renamed files), suspicious email behavior (phishing from compromised accounts, outbound email spikes), and abnormal data sharing (large external transfers, unexpected downloads). Attackers often exfiltrate data before deploying ransomware to increase ransom pressure. The post emphasizes proactive, real-time monitoring across Google Workspace and Microsoft 365 environments, and promotes ManagedMethods' Cloud Monitor as a centralized solution for detecting these threats early.
